1	// basics task: ci-performance — the weekly read on where this repo's CI time goes,
2	// and whether it has got worse.
3	//
4	// A suite's runtime degrades the way a lawn grows: never in one visible step, so
5	// nobody profiles it until it is bad enough to complain about, by which point the
6	// cause is a dozen changes back. This task takes the measurement on a cadence
7	// instead, from the one ledger that cannot be argued with — the Actions run
8	// history — and keeps a standing record of it.
9	//
10	// CONDITIONAL HANDOFF. Code-work does the measuring, which is pure code: read the
11	// runs, take each workflow's median over this window and the one before, compare.
12	// A quiet week ends there — the record is refreshed and no agent is spent. Only a
13	// real regression requests the agent, which then has something worth its time: a
14	// named workflow, a before and after, and the ci-performance-evaluation skill's
15	// method for finding the cause.
16	//
17	// WHY sonnet: the finding arrives already localized to a workflow and a delta, and
18	// the skill states the method step by step; what remains is profiling and a bounded
19	// fix. Ceilinged at `open-pr`, so a change to how this repo builds or tests always
20	// lands in front of a reviewer.
21	//
22	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
23	
24	export default {
25	  id: 'ci-performance',
26	  frequency: 'weekly',
27	  // Movement, not standing state: CI runtime only changes when something lands, so
28	  // a week with no commits and no PR activity has nothing new to measure — the same
29	  // runs, the same medians, the same verdict as last week.
30	  precondition_signals: ['commits', 'prs'],
31	  agent_model: 'sonnet',
32	  expected_outcome: 'pr',
33	  automerge: 'anything',             // CI itself is the gate: a fix that turns anything red cannot merge, and a green one is the point (owner, 2026-08-30)
34	  agent_instructions: 'task.md',
35	  code_work: 'node worker.mjs',
36	  // A couple of hundred run records plus one job breakdown, against this repo's own
37	  // API. Seconds in practice; the bound is for a rate-limited or wedged read.
38	  code_work_timeout: 300,
39	  // Profiling a suite means running it, more than once, in both arms of an A/B.
40	  agent_execution_timeout: 3600,
41	
42	  precondition(signals) {
43	    const commits = signals.commits?.count ?? 0;
44	    const prs = (signals.prs?.touched ?? []).length;
45	    if (commits === 0 && prs === 0) {
46	      return { run: false, reason: 'no commits and no PR activity this week — CI ran on nothing new, so its timings cannot have moved' };
47	    }
48	    return { run: true, reason: `${commits} commit(s) and ${prs} touched PR(s) this week — re-measure CI timings and compare against the previous window` };
49	  },
50	};
51

1	// jwt task: jwt-advisory-watch — the one JWT concern that moves with the
2	// outside world rather than with this repo's commits. JWT libraries have a
3	// history of critical vulnerabilities (the alg:none era hit several at once),
4	// and a repo that never touches its lockfile still becomes vulnerable the day
5	// an advisory publishes. So the watch is a MONTHLY floor, deliberately
6	// ungated on repo movement: the trigger lives outside the repo, so there is
7	// no signal to gate on (contrast tidy-prs, whose verdicts only change when a
8	// PR moves). Worker: task.md. Assess-only: a run that finds an affected version
9	// files an issue naming it; a clean run writes nothing at all, and never opens a
10	// PR or edits a manifest.
11	//
12	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
13	
14	export default {
15	  id: 'jwt-advisory-watch',
16	  frequency: 'monthly',                     // an advisory watch is a floor, not an alert channel
17	  precondition_signals: [],                 // the trigger is the outside world — nothing repo-side gates it
18	  agent_model: 'sonnet',                    // version-range vs advisory-range comparison is a judgment call
19	  expected_outcome: 'none',                 // assess-only: opens an ISSUE for a hit, never a PR
20	  agent_instructions: 'task.md',
21	  agent_execution_timeout: 900,             // a handful of manifest reads and advisory lookups
22	
23	  precondition() {
24	    return {
25	      run: true,
26	      reason: 'JWT library advisories publish on the outside world\'s clock — the monthly sweep runs unconditionally',
27	      context: ['Check the repo\'s JWT/JOSE libraries against published security advisories (read-only — file an issue for a hit, never change a manifest).'],
28	    };
29	  },
30	};
31

1	// claudinite-dashboard task: deploy-oauth-exchange — put the dashboard's sign-in
2	// endpoint live, and prove the deployed URL answers.
3	//
4	// `frequency: 'manual'` — nothing recurring is being asked. The endpoint changes
5	// when its source changes, when the app's client secret is rotated, or when the set
6	// of page origins allowed to call it changes; none of those is a cadence, so the
7	// scheduler never instantiates this and the only way it runs is a work item created
8	// by hand:
9	//
10	//   create-work-item claudinite-dashboard/deploy-oauth-exchange
11	//
12	// `agent_model: 'none'` — pure code. Read the endpoint's source out of the mount,
13	// upload it with its bindings, route it, probe it, report the URL.
14	//
15	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
16	
17	export default {
18	  id: 'deploy-oauth-exchange',
19	  frequency: 'manual',
20	  precondition_signals: [],
21	  agent_model: 'none',
22	  // It writes nothing in this repo. The one edit the deployment implies — naming
23	  // the minted URL as `exchangeUrl` — is the member's own declaration, and the run
24	  // reports it rather than making it.
25	  expected_outcome: 'none',
26	  code_work: 'node worker.mjs',
27	  // Three API calls and a probe that waits out route propagation (six attempts,
28	  // five seconds apart). The bound is that probe's worst case with room around it.
29	  code_work_timeout: 300,
30	  // The two real credentials, and only those. CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN needs exactly one
31	  // grant — Account · Workers Scripts · Edit — on the account hosting the endpoint;
32	  // GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET is the App's client secret. The client id is public and
33	  // lives in the declaration; the Cloudflare account id is a repository VARIABLE, which
34	  // every task's code-work is handed with nothing declared, so listing it here would
35	  // both misstate it as sensitive and put it in a store it does not need.
36	  required_secrets: ['CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN', 'GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET'],
37	
38	  // Never due on its own: an item exists only because somebody created one, and
39	  // that IS the request. A `false` here would close the operator's own item without
40	  // running it, with no anchor to roll to.
41	  precondition() {
42	    return { run: true, reason: 'a work item for this manual lever exists, which is the request to deploy' };
43	  },
44	};
45

1	// claudinite-fleet-sheepdog task: fleet-add-missing-packs — get every member declaring the packs it
2	// is missing. The fourth fleet question, now fully on the FAN-OUT model (#749).
3	//
4	// `agent_model: 'none'` — this task runs no agent, HERE. Its first incarnation ended
5	// in an enforcer-side agent stage that ran adopt-pack against members, and it failed
6	// in production the first time it ran: the enforcer's executor is (correctly) scoped
7	// to the enforcer repo alone, and "the enforcer's session is provisioned with the
8	// fleet" turned out to be an assumption, not a fact. The agentic work moved to where
9	// the access already is: each member's own adopt-requested-packs task
10	// (claudinite-growth). This task DISPATCHES — it converges a work-list issue in
11	// the member and fires that member's scheduler — and the member EXECUTES, with the
12	// repo checked out, under its own declaration's guards. No agent anywhere needs
13	// cross-repo access.
14	//
15	// TWO WAYS A PACK COMES TO BE MISSING, and the task is PARAMETERISED over them
16	// rather than split in two, because they differ only in how the work list is made:
17	//   scan_for_needed_packs=true   nobody has decided anything: fingerprint every
18	//                                member's shape and SUSPECT what its declaration
19	//                                does not carry. What the weekly run sends.
20	//   ADD_PACKS=<ids>              the owner already decided: REQUEST these packs,
21	//                                with this config and these interview answers, in
22	//                                these named repos. What a FORCED run sends, through
23	//                                the item's Context — see worker.mjs for
24	//                                the full override set and params.mjs for why
25	//                                neither parameter has a default.
26	// Both converge the same protocol issues (protocol.mjs) and fire the same
27	// member-side task.
28	//
29	// WHERE THE FLEET REACH COMES FROM: FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN, the account-spanning PAT —
30	// with Actions WRITE, because firing another repo's scheduler is an Actions write.
31	// No session scope, no executor grant: the one credential is the PAT, and the only
32	// things that cross a repo boundary are an issue and a workflow_dispatch.
33	//
34	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
35	
36	export default {
37	  id: 'fleet-add-missing-packs',
38	  frequency: 'weekly',                   // a repo's shape is slow-moving — the same cadence growth-discover-packs uses for the same reason
39	  precondition_signals: [],              // no signal — every input is another repo's tree, which no per-repo collector can see
40	  agent_model: 'none',                   // pure code here: scan/request, converge member issues, fire member schedulers — the AGENT is the member's own
41	  expected_outcome: 'none',              // it writes issues in MEMBERS and queues their runs; no PR here, ever
42	  // The weekly run's PARAMETERS, sent explicitly on the command line rather than
43	  // defaulted inside the worker (params.mjs): the declaration is where a reader looks
44	  // first to learn what the cadence does, so what the cadence does is written here.
45	  // `all-covered-members` is a keyword the caller sends, not a fallback the worker
46	  // assumes — no call site can reach the whole fleet by omission.
47	  code_work: 'node worker.mjs --scan-for-needed-packs=true --repos=all-covered-members',
48	  // One tree listing per member plus a bounded handful of content reads per
49	  // content-reading fingerprint, plus the per-member issue convergence and one
50	  // dispatch POST per member with findings, all serial with a secondary rate limit.
51	  // The same 900s the other sweeps carry: ~10x the expected walk.
52	  code_work_timeout: 900,
53	  required_secrets: ['FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN'], // the account-spanning PAT; fleet-token.mjs states the grant
54	
55	  // Fire weekly unconditionally. Every input lives OUTSIDE this repo — another
56	  // member's tree, another member's declaration — and no per-repo collector can see
57	  // any of them, so there is no signal that would tell us in advance whether the
58	  // answer changed. Cheap to no-op: a fleet that declares what it should converges
59	  // nothing, fires nobody, and the run is one read-only sweep.
60	  //
61	  // A hand-created item runs this precondition too (the queue evaluates it at pick,
62	  // tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6.4), and it says yes unconditionally — so what makes a
63	  // forced run different is its Context, not a bypass: the parameters there are what
64	  // run this task as something other than its weekly self.
65	  precondition() {
66	    return { run: true, reason: 'weekly fleet scan for packs a member is missing (no-ops cheaply on a fleet whose members already declare what their shape suspects)' };
67	  },
68	};

1	// claudinite-fleet-sheepdog task: fleet-baseline — the enforcer's MANUAL lever: force every covered
2	// member (or the ones named) to baseline NOW instead of at its next anchor.
3	//
4	// `frequency: 'manual'` — the first task on the non-cadence (#749). It answers no
5	// recurring question, so the scheduler run never instantiates it; the ONLY way it runs is a
6	// work item created by hand, optionally carrying its parameters as Context lines:
7	//
8	//   create-work-item claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline
9	//   --context "REPOS=Alpha Beta"        (optional — omit for every covered member; space-separated)
10	//   --context "DRY_RUN=true"            (optional — report what would fire, fire nothing)
11	//   --context "INCLUDE_DORMANT=true"    (optional — dormant members are skipped by default)
12	//   --context "FOLLOW_MINUTES=30"       (optional — how long to follow members to current)
13	//
14	// This replaces the pack's standalone fleet-baseline WORKFLOW (retired 2026-08-11,
15	// #749). The workflow existed for two reasons that are both gone: its FOLLOW half
16	// (watch every member to a terminal state — a 45-minute sleep no serialized run
17	// should hold) is given up, and its typed `workflow_dispatch` inputs are carried by
18	// the item's Context instead. What the workflow shape COST is what this shape
19	// recovers: the `.github/` managed copy was the one file the nightly converge could
20	// not push (#649's withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path), while a task rides the
21	// ordinary vendor refresh like everything else.
22	//
23	// `agent_model: 'none'` — pure code. The whole pass is the dispatch sweep
24	// (force-fleet-baseline.mjs, invoked by worker.mjs): enumerate the fleet over the
25	// PAT, wake each covered member's own `update` item, follow each one until it stamps
26	// canon's published versions, and report the full roster by OUTCOME (#1293). Nothing
27	// agentic happens HERE — each member's own converge may hand off to that member's own
28	// agent, which is the fan-out model's point: the enforcer dispatches, the member
29	// executes, and no agent anywhere needs cross-repo access.
30	//
31	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
32	
33	export default {
34	  id: 'fleet-baseline',
35	  frequency: 'manual',                   // an operator lever — never due on any cadence, runs only when forced
36	  precondition_signals: [],              // no signal — nothing recurring to predict
37	  agent_model: 'none',                   // pure code: enumerate, fire, report (task-code-work DESIGN §4)
38	  expected_outcome: 'none',              // it queues Actions runs in MEMBERS; it writes nothing here or there
39	  code_work: 'node worker.mjs',
40	  // The dispatch half is one enumeration plus a declaration read and one POST per
41	  // member — under a minute. What sizes this bound is the FOLLOW (#1293): the sweep
42	  // stays until every dispatched member stamps canon's versions, and a member's own
43	  // update takes 5–10 minutes end to end. The follow gives up at
44	  // DEFAULT_FOLLOW_MINUTES (20) and reports what it was still waiting on, so this
45	  // must sit above that with room for the dispatch walk and the final probe —
46	  // otherwise the platform kills the run at the bound and the report is never
47	  // printed, which is the one outcome worse than a slow one.
48	  code_work_timeout: 1800,
49	  required_secrets: ['FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN'], // the account-spanning PAT; fleet-token.mjs states the grant
50	
51	  // Never due on its own — `manual` means the scheduler run never instantiates this task,
52	  // so an item exists ONLY because a human created one, and that IS the request.
53	  // Hence run: true. The queue evaluates this verdict at pick (tasks-dispatch
54	  // DESIGN §6.4), unlike the slot mechanism where a forced run bypassed it; a
55	  // no-go here has no anchor to roll to, so it would close the operator's own
56	  // item `task:obsolete` without running. Answering `false` is how this lever
57	  // stopped working at the flip.
58	  precondition() {
59	    return { run: true, reason: 'a work item for this manual lever exists, which is the request to run it' };
60	  },
61	};

3	// pass is deterministic code the executor runs as code-work — no agent, no dispatch
4	// issue. The worker calls its sibling, the sweep (check-fleet-pack-seeds.mjs): read
5	// every covered member's declaration and add the seeds it lacks.

8	// about the FLEET rather than about that repo. Canon cannot supply it — a bootstrap run
9	// does not know which fleet it is bootstrapping into — and one fleet's value hardcoded
10	// in shared code is exactly the coupling packs exist to prevent. The enforcer can: it

12	// declare, and the sweep converges that list across them.

14	// IT NAMES NO PACK. Every id comes from this repo's own config; the task and its sweep

16	// config, not this pack.

18	// THE ONE SWEEP IN THIS PACK THAT WRITES. The others report a condition and converge an
19	// issue for a human; a seed carries no human decision (the fleet already made it, in
20	// this repo's config), so an issue asking someone to copy it into every member would be
21	// ceremony around a mechanical edit. Hence `expected_outcome: 'none'`: the write goes to
22	// OTHER repos, not this one, and the outcome ceiling describes what a task may do to its
23	// OWN repo — this task opens no PR here at all.
24	//
25	// CLASSIFICATION (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §6, the same note the other sweeps
26	// carry): an ORDINARY PACK TASK, not a fleet mechanism. Its *implementation* reaches
27	// every repo under the owner over a PAT, but its declaration, scheduling and lifecycle
28	// are exactly those of any pack task — it is active because this repo declares the
29	// claudinite-fleet-sheepdog pack, and it runs however this repo's tasks run. Hence no
30	// `session_scope: 'fleet'` and no `fleet` signal: those describe how a task is WIRED,
31	// and nothing about this task's wiring is fleet-shaped.
32	//
33	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.

35	export default {
36	  id: 'fleet-pack-seeds',
37	  frequency: 'daily',                    // a member becomes writable the moment its nightly converge vendors the pack — daily is what turns that into "the next morning"
38	  precondition_signals: [],              // no signal — the sweep reads the fleet itself, over the PAT
39	  agent_model: 'none',                   // pure code — no agent (task-code-work DESIGN §4)
40	  expected_outcome: 'none',              // it writes to MEMBERS, never to this repo: no PR here, ever
41	  code_work: 'node worker.mjs',
42	  // Two or three REST reads per member (declaration, whether each seeded pack is on its
43	  // disk, and one PUT for the members being written) plus the enumeration, all serial,

45	  // carry, for the same reason: ~10x the expected walk while staying inside the hourly
46	  // cadence.
47	  code_work_timeout: 900,
48	  required_secrets: ['FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN'], // the account-spanning PAT; fleet-token.mjs states the grant
49	
50	  // Fire daily unconditionally. Every input lives OUTSIDE this repo — another member's

52	  // there is no signal that would say in advance whether the answer changed. The sweep
53	  // is cheap to no-op: a fleet whose members already declare its seeds reads each one
54	  // and writes nothing, and a fleet that seeds nothing stops before the walk.
55	  precondition() {

1	// claudinite-fleet-sheepdog task: fleet-roster — one walk of the fleet answering the enforcer's two
2	// standing questions about every repo under the owner (#788):
3	//
4	//   is this repo a MEMBER?                        → `fleet-adoption` issues
5	//   is that membership still MEANING anything?    → `fleet-drift` issues
6	//
7	// `agent_model: 'none'` with `code_work: 'node worker.mjs'`: the whole pass is
8	// deterministic code the executor runs as code-work — no agent phase.
9	// The worker calls its sibling, the sweep (check-fleet-roster.mjs), which enumerates
10	// the fleet once, reads each repo's declaration once, and hands the resulting roster to
11	// the two issue families (adoption-issues.mjs, drift-issues.mjs).
12	//
13	// WHY ONE TASK. These were two — a daily `fleet-census` and a weekly `fleet-freshness`
14	// — and each carried its own enumeration, its own structural skips and its own
15	// declaration read per repo. The freshness half's own header said it "takes coverage as
16	// given" while in fact re-deriving it on another cadence in another process, so the two
17	// classifications could disagree and did. One walk means one membership verdict per
18	// repo, one report, and one failure boundary.
19	//
20	// WHY DAILY, and what it costs. The freshness question was weekly because drift is
21	// measured in DAYS and a daily re-ask could not change its answer. Merged, that
22	// argument buys nothing: the walk runs daily for the coverage question regardless, and
23	// the alternative — half the task gated on a weekly cadence it computed itself — would
24	// reimplement dueness, which the engine owns (the scheduler run instantiates a task's item
25	// when its anchor comes) and which is not a thing a task can ask about from inside
26	// itself. So the freshness probe now runs daily too: roughly two extra REST
27	// reads per covered member on the six days that used to be coverage-only. The merge is
28	// not an API-call saving and is not claimed as one — what it buys is one roster instead
29	// of two that can disagree. Drift converging within a day rather than a week is the
30	// side benefit, and convergeDrift's silence on an unchanged verdict is what keeps the
31	// faster cadence from turning every thread into a wall of identical notes.
32	//
33	// CLASSIFICATION (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §6, the same note RULES.md carries):
34	// this is an ORDINARY PACK TASK, not a fleet mechanism. Its *implementation* happens to
35	// scan every repo under the owner over a PAT, but its declaration, scheduling and
36	// lifecycle are exactly those of any pack task — it is active because this repo declares
37	// the claudinite-fleet-sheepdog pack, and it runs however this repo's tasks run. Hence no `fleet` signal
38	// and no session scope of its own (the PACK declares the executor reach): those describe
39	// how a task is WIRED, and nothing about this task's wiring is fleet-shaped. The
40	// cross-repo reach lives in the implementation, never in the declaration.
41	//
42	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
43	
44	export default {
45	  id: 'fleet-roster',
46	  frequency: 'daily',                    // the coverage question's cadence — a repo created, adopted or archived under the owner should not wait a week
47	  precondition_signals: [],              // no signal — the sweep reads the fleet itself, over the PAT
48	  agent_model: 'none',                   // pure code — no agent (task-code-work DESIGN §4)
49	  expected_outcome: 'none',              // the honest ceiling: it opens ADOPTION and DRIFT issues, never a PR — it reports, it does not repair
50	  code_work: 'node worker.mjs',
51	  // The walk covers EVERY repo in the fleet: one paged enumeration, one declaration
52	  // read per repo, two further reads per measured member (scheduler workflow, canon
53	  // compare), then both issue convergences — all serial, and a secondary rate limit
54	  // makes it slower still. The same 900s both predecessors carried: ~10x the expected
55	  // walk while staying well inside the hourly scheduler cadence, so a hung sweep is
56	  // killed long before the next run could collide with it.
57	  code_work_timeout: 900,
58	  required_secrets: ['FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN'], // the account-spanning PAT; fleet-token.mjs states the grant
59	
60	  // Fire daily unconditionally. Every input lives OUTSIDE this repo — another repo's
61	  // declaration, another member's workflow, canon's head — and no per-repo collector
62	  // can see any of them, so there is no signal that would tell us in advance whether
63	  // either answer changed. Cheap to no-op: a converged fleet opens and closes nothing,
64	  // and an unhealthy member that is unhealthy for the same reason is not even
65	  // commented on.
66	  precondition() {
67	    return { run: true, reason: 'daily fleet roster sweep — coverage and freshness in one walk (converges adoption and drift issues; no-ops cheaply on a converged fleet)' };
68	  },
69	};

1	// growth-discover-packs — the FLEET sweep for technologies the canon does not yet
2	// home. One weekly pass over every member: read what the fleet is actually built
3	// on, subtract what the canon's packs/ shelf already homes, and open a reviewed PR
4	// authoring the missing pack.
5	//
6	// The only pack-authoring stage there is. A member does not mint packs of its
7	// own — its local packs are what adoption seeded, and growth-extract writes
8	// rules into those — so a technology no canon pack homes is noticed and homed
9	// here or nowhere.
10	//
11	// Central because ONE run sees every member: first-sight dedup is trivial — the
12	// third member using a technology is recognised as the same gap as the first,
13	// with no cross-run state. That was the argument for keeping this central when
14	// everything else moved per-repo.
15	//
16	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
17	
18	export default {
19	  id: 'growth-discover-packs',
20	  frequency: 'weekly',                   // the fleet's stacks are slow-moving — a weekly sweep, not a daily one
21	  precondition_signals: ['fleet'],       // canon-only aggregate: who the members are and what they declare
22	  // This task reads every member's tree, which an ordinary session in this repo does
23	  // not reach. Reach is a property of WHICH endpoint the hand-off calls, so a task
24	  // needing more than an ordinary session names one; the key resolves in this repo's
25	  // own config, and until it is configured the hand-off converges the item to triage
26	  // naming what is missing.
27	  invocation_endpoint: 'fleet',
28	  agent_model: 'opus',                   // judging what is genuinely canon-worthy and authoring a pack is heavy judgment
29	  expected_outcome: 'pr',
30	  automerge: 'nothing',              // a new canon pack every repo will read — owner-approved, never auto-merged
31	  agent_instructions: 'task.md',
32	  agent_execution_timeout: 3600,         // manifest N members' stacks + author a pack — a generous weekly bound, extreme protection
33	
34	  // Fire on the covered members, every week. There is no windowed trigger: the
35	  // opportunity is standing (a technology the fleet uses that no canon pack
36	  // homes), not a recent change, so the sweep runs weekly and no-ops cheaply
37	  // when nothing is unhomed. A member with a parsable declaration but no declared
38	  // packs is not running Claudinite in any usable sense — the same test the fleet
39	  // reader uses before it probes a member — so it is not swept.
40	  precondition(signals) {
41	    const fleet = signals.fleet;
42	    if (!fleet) return { run: false, reason: 'no fleet signal (FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN unset, or this repo is not a canon home)' };
43	    if (fleet.error) return { run: false, reason: `fleet enumeration failed — ${fleet.error} (sweeping nothing on unproven fleet state)` };
44	    const members = (fleet.members ?? []).filter((m) => m.activePacks.length);
45	    if (!members.length) return { run: false, reason: 'no covered member to sweep' };
46	    const repos = members.map((m) => m.repo);
47	    return {
48	      run: true,
49	      reason: `weekly canon pack-discovery sweep over ${members.length} covered member(s)`,
50	      context: [
51	        `Members to sweep: ${repos.join(', ')}.`,
52	        'Read ONLY these members — do not enumerate the fleet yourself or widen past this list.',
53	      ],
54	    };
55	  },
56	};

1	// growth-promote — the growth lifecycle's CENTRAL stage. Reads the participating
2	// members' local packs, generalizes the portable lessons, and opens an owner-gated
3	// PR against the canon. A fleet-reaching task: it runs on the canon home repo's own
4	// scheduler, and its precondition reads the `fleet` signal — the members aggregate
5	// over the fleet PAT.
6	//
7	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
8	//
9	// "Central, once" is enforced by declaration cardinality, not orchestrator wiring:
10	// a canon is declared by its one home repo, so this task exists nowhere else. No
11	// barrier — promote reads whatever is already MERGED on members' default branches,
12	// so a lesson extracted tonight is promoted on the same run when its auto-merge
13	// landed in time, else the next one.
14	
15	export default {
16	  id: 'growth-promote',
17	  frequency: 'daily',
18	  // THE CROSS-REPO HALF IS THIS REPO'S OWN scheduler anchor, not a field here. Promote reads what
19	  // has already merged on MEMBERS' default branches, and `schedule_after:` only ever matches an item
20	  // in this repo's own queue — so the members-extract-then-canon-promotes ordering has no declarable
21	  // form and lives in the anchor: a canon home sets its daily hour after its members'.
22	  //
23	  // The WITHIN-repo half is declarable, and is: a canon home is a member too, so its own extract must
24	  // settle before promote reads the local packs it just wrote. A canon that does not declare
25	  // claudinite-growth queues no such item, and the ordering is then vacuous rather than blocking.
26	  schedule_after: ['claudinite-growth/growth-extract'],
27	  precondition_signals: ['fleet'],       // canon-only aggregate: which members changed their local packs
28	  // This task reads every member's local packs, which an ordinary session in this
29	  // repo does not reach. Reach is a property of WHICH endpoint the hand-off calls,
30	  // so a task needing more than an ordinary session names one; the key resolves in
31	  // this repo's own config, and until it is configured the hand-off converges the
32	  // item to triage naming what is missing.
33	  invocation_endpoint: 'fleet',
34	  agent_model: 'opus',                   // portability, dedup-vs-corpus, and routing are the heaviest judgment
35	  expected_outcome: 'pr',
36	  automerge: 'nothing',              // the judgment gate before shared canon — owner-approved, never auto-merged
37	  agent_instructions: 'task.md',
38	  agent_execution_timeout: 2700,         // reading N members + generalizing + authoring a PR — generous bound, extreme protection
39	
40	  // Fire when a participating member changed its local packs in the window. A
41	  // participant declares claudinite-growth and carries local packs (the only
42	  // source promote reads); the growth entry's `{ config: { promote: false } }`
43	  // opts a member out of promotion while it keeps extracting/deduping locally
44	  // (absent or true = participate). A member whose local packs didn't move in the
45	  // window has nothing new to lift up — so the daily trigger targets exactly the
46	  // changed set, and the executor's Context binds the worker to those members.
47	  precondition(signals) {
48	    const fleet = signals.fleet;
49	    if (!fleet) return { run: false, reason: 'no fleet signal (FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN unset, or this repo is not a canon home)' };
50	    if (fleet.error) return { run: false, reason: `fleet enumeration failed — ${fleet.error} (retiring/promoting nothing on unproven fleet state)` };
51	    const participants = (fleet.members ?? [])
52	      .filter((m) => m.activePacks.includes('claudinite-growth') && m.hasLocalPacks)
53	      .filter((m) => m.packConfigs?.['claudinite-growth']?.promote !== false);
54	    const changed = participants.filter((m) => m.localPacksChanged);
55	    if (!changed.length) return { run: false, reason: 'no participating member changed its local packs in the window' };
56	    const repos = changed.map((m) => m.repo);
57	    return {
58	      run: true,
59	      reason: `${changed.length} participating member(s) changed their local packs in the window`,
60	      context: [
61	        `Target members (local packs changed in the window): ${repos.join(', ')}.`,
62	        'Read ONLY these members\' local packs — do not enumerate the fleet yourself or widen past this list.',
63	      ],
64	    };
65	  },
66	};

1	// The request implementer (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §16) — the engine's one built-in
2	// task, and the only one that may read an item's `Model`.
3	//
4	// A person marks an ordinary issue `task:origin:ad-hoc`; the scheduler run adopts
5	// it by writing the machine block onto that issue and applying the first status —
6	// the issue IS the item (§16.1); this task's precondition decides, at pickup,
7	// whether the run happens; the session implements the issue and leaves a pull
8	// request. There is no code-work phase at all: the authorization a worker would
9	// have performed is the precondition's, and the item's `Request:` field — which
10	// names the item's own issue — is the whole payload.
11	
12	// Push permission, as the permission API answers it. `triage` and `read` are
13	// deliberately not here: the ask was push access, and a read-only collaborator
14	// rides every webhook payload as `COLLABORATOR` (F30).
15	export const PUSH_PERMISSIONS = ['admin', 'maintain', 'write'];
16	
17	// Who, if anyone, with push access asked for this. Pure over the `request` signal's
18	// read, so the judgment is testable without GitHub and the reads stay where every
19	// other read is.
20	export function eligibility(req) {
21	  if (PUSH_PERMISSIONS.includes(req.authorPermission)) {
22	    return { ok: true, why: `opened by @${req.author}, who has push access` };
23	  }
24	  const blessed = (req.approvals ?? []).find((a) => PUSH_PERMISSIONS.includes(a.permission));
25	  if (blessed) return { ok: true, why: `approved by @${blessed.login} with \`/claude go\`` };
26	  return { ok: false, why: 'neither opened nor approved with `/claude go` by anyone with push access on this repository' };
27	}
28	
29	export default {
30	  // The literal, not the constant beside it in `built-in-tasks.mjs`: the
31	  // declaration-shape check reads this file statically and cannot resolve an
32	  // import. The two are pinned to each other in request-mode.test.mjs.
33	  id: 'implement-request',
34	  // MANUAL: the scheduler run never puts this on a calendar. An item exists only because an
35	  // issue was marked, which is what makes a request a first-class origin of work
36	  // rather than a schedule nobody asked for.

content.text:
I've now read all 25 task declarations, the automerge policy engine, the signal collectors, and the task contract. Here's the assessment.

## What the automerge system actually is

`packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs` gives the `automerge` declaration three layers: whole-policy words (`nothing`/`anything`), a **flat namespace of named rules** (built-ins like `doc-changes`, pack-declared ones via `merge-rules.json`), and **combinators** — a list is a union, `&&` intersects, `reject:` vetoes, `under:<dir>` is a parameterized inline term. Unknown names fail closed, and one evaluator serves both judging surfaces.

## The precondition inventory (25 tasks)

- **Unconditional `run: true` — 11 tasks.** The 4 manual levers (`adopt-requested-packs`, `fleet-baseline`, `deploy-oauth-exchange`, `verify-production`: "an item exists, which is the request"), the 3 fleet sweeps + `task-janitor` ("inputs live outside the repo / cheap to no-op"), and 3 calendar-unconditional agentic tasks (`rule-revalidation`, `prose-to-checks-sweep`, `jwt-advisory-watch` — "the world's clock, not the repo's"). The last group spends **opus/sonnet unconditionally**, silent repo or not.
- **Movement-gated — 9 tasks**, all composed from the same few signal reads: `commits.substantiveChange` (growth-extract, improve-comments, tidy-issues' widener, store-release's second arm), `commits.count > 0 || fresh log` (usage-fold), `commits || prs.touched` (ci-performance), `issues.touched` minus `task:*` items (tidy-issues), `open && touched` (tidy-prs), `localPacks.present && (mount moved || local changed)` (growth-dedup).
- **Standing-state / threshold gates**: `stamp.present` (update), `oldestLogAgeDays > retentionDays` (logs-prune), `manifestVersion ≠ latestTag` (store-release), **pending-PR vetoes** (improve-comments by title prefix, wiki-growth by path prefix with fail-closed unknown).
- **Fleet-filtered — 2** (growth-promote, growth-discover-packs): filter `fleet.members`, emit the member list as binding context.
- **Genuine code — 1**: `implement-request`'s push-permission eligibility check, a security boundary with three-valued verdicts.

So yes — the shapes repeat heavily, and roughly **22–24 of 25 preconditions are expressible in a ~15-term vocabulary** with the same combinator grammar automerge already taught everyone: list = OR (independent reasons to run), `&&` = AND, a veto prefix (`while:` / `unless:`, the mirror of `reject:`), and parameterized terms (`pr-pending-under:<dir>`, `pr-pending-titled:<prefix>`, `touched-outside:<dir>`). Reasons and most `context` lines (touched-issue lists, member lists, path scopes with a cap) fall out of the terms generically. A `precondition` **function stays legal** for the residue — `implement-request` should never be data.

Two deliberate inversions from automerge, both forced by existing lessons:

- **Fail direction.** Automerge fails closed to "nothing merges" — safe. A precondition that fails closed to "skip" is permanent silent staleness (the update task's #1344 lesson, and F27). An unresolvable term must return `{ error }` — a loud run failure, never a quiet decline.
- **Delivery sequencing.** Old engines must not meet declarative preconditions they can't evaluate (the SPEC_KEYS lesson, #1400): the engine capability ships and fields first; canon task declarations convert after. Member-local task files convert on their own clock — the function form stays accepted forever, like the legacy field spellings already do.

## The silent-repo requirement

The right home is a standard term, `repo-active` — any of: substantive commit, non-task issue/PR touch, session captured, in the window — **implied as a conjunct on every declarative precondition**, with an explicit exemption term for tasks whose input genuinely isn't the repo. Exemption candidates are exactly the documented ones: the manual levers (a filed item is the mandate), `update` (its input is the canon, and declining wrongly costs unrepairable staleness), the fleet sweeps (inputs are other repos), `logs-prune` (age is the trigger), `task-janitor`. The tasks whose behavior actually **changes** are the calendar-unconditional agentic ones — `rule-revalidation`, `prose-to-checks-sweep`, `jwt-advisory-watch`, `wiki-growth` — which today burn a model run weekly/monthly on a repo nobody works in. Gating them on repo-activity is, I believe, the point of your requirement.

One gap in the current "silence" classifier: your definition says **a PR from a scheduled task is still silent**. Today's exclusions are a title regex (`HOUSEKEEPING`), bot authors, and corpus-only paths — which miss task PRs with plain titles landing outside `.claudinite/` (a ci-performance fix, a wiki-growth page). The robust fix is structural: have the task delivery lane stamp a `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` commit trailer on every task-authored commit, and key the `repo-active` classifier on it (keeping the regexes for history already in the window).

A few decisions are yours before I build anything:

options.label: Gate them (Recommended)

options.description: The advisory watch keeps its unconditional monthly floor (a dormant repo can still become vulnerable); the other three gate on activity.
options.label: Gate all except jwt-advisory-watch

options.description: They keep their documented world's-clock rationale; the silence gate only formalizes what movement-gated tasks already do.
options.label: Exempt all four

questions.question: Gate the calendar-unconditional agentic tasks (rule-revalidation, prose-to-checks-sweep, jwt-advisory-watch, wiki-growth) on repo activity too? This is the one real behavior change: today they run on the world's clock regardless of repo silence.

options.description: The delivery lane stamps `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` on every task-authored commit; the repo-active classifier keys on the trailer, keeping today's title regexes only for pre-existing history.
options.label: Structural trailer (Recommended)

options.description: Extend the existing HOUSEKEEPING regex to cover the leaking task PR titles (ci-performance, wiki-growth) — cheaper, but every new task title is a new leak.
options.label: Title/author regexes only

# Writing migration and implementation plans

A plan's phases are not a narrative of the work; they are a **schedule of who has to be present
when**. Ordering them by topic — "phase 1: the store, phase 2: the workers, phase 3: cutover" —
scatters the moments that need a human across the whole run, and every one of them stops it. Order
them by *what blocks*, and the run ends with a stretch nobody has to attend.

The shape this produces, in one line: **setup, then one approval of everything, then a chain that
runs itself.** All the code is written before the owner is asked for anything — the cleanup and
the destructive tail included — so their attention is spent once; and every step after that
approval is a queued continuation armed on the step before it, so the migration advances without
anyone remembering it exists.

Everything below assumes the change is already agreed: the problem, and that this migration is the
right way to solve it (basics' *Starting any requested change*). The end-state's **shape** —
converging in one forced pass, accepting legacy input at the door, a standing mechanism for
stragglers — is [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Planning a migration*; this skill is the ordering.

## Two deliverables, two homes — and only two

An initiative produces at most one document and one issue, and neither may do the
other's job:

- **The design doc** (`docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md`, where the project keeps one)
  describes the **end state and its rationale** — what the mechanism is once the
  work is done, and why that shape over the alternatives, with each alternative's
  drawbacks stated. It never carries the previous state as narrative, the requests
  or conversation that led here, owner attributions or opinions, progress, or a
  phase list. The test: a reader who arrives after the migration finishes must
  find nothing to delete. Legacy shapes appear only where the end state itself
  keeps handling them (a decode map, an accepted input) — as mechanism, not as
  history.
- **The migration is work, not a document.** Its plan lives in the tracking issue
  and nowhere else — never a plan or migration document committed to the repo. A
  plan document goes stale the moment work starts and cannot be checked off; the
  issue is checkable, append-only, and dies with the work.

## The three blocks, and where each belongs

Sort every step of the plan into one of three kinds, and let that sort — not the subject matter —
decide the phase it lands in.

**1. Out-of-band setup — before any code changes.** Anything performed outside the repo that a
later step will need: provisioning an environment, creating a session or runner, setting a secret
or variable, granting a permission, flipping a platform setting, registering a webhook. Nearly all
of it is **non-destructive** — it adds a capability that nothing yet consumes, so doing it early
costs nothing and changes no behaviour. Doing it *late* costs the whole run: the plan reaches the
step that reads the secret and stops until someone is available.

Front-load all of it into phase zero, before the first line of code. Write it as its own issue
with a checkbox per step (basics' *Handing over a human-only step*), stating for each what stays
broken while it is off, and written per
[writing-handover-issues](../writing-handover-issues/SKILL.md). And before writing it down, confirm you genuinely cannot do it yourself —
a step handed to a human that you could have taken is the most expensive kind of block there is.

The exception is the genuinely destructive step — deleting the old store, revoking the old
credential, removing the compatibility shim. Those are not setup; they are the migration's tail,
and they belong after the cutover has been observed working — which is **not** a later phase. A
cleanup phase falls due long after the run that would have done it ended, and nothing brings it
back.

**Write its code anyway, now, in the stack** (the next sort), so the owner approves it with
everything else — and make its *merge* a link in the chain below, armed on the cutover being
observed. What must never be deferred is the writing and the approving; what must always be
deferred is the merging.

**2. Review and authorization gates — collapsed into one pass.** Every phase that ships code is a
gate: the owner must read it and approve it before the next phase can start. A plan with four
coding phases has four such waits, and each one is dead time whose length nobody controls.

Write **all** the code first — every phase of it, including the cleanup and the destructive tail —
as a stack of PRs each based on the previous, and put the whole stack in front of the owner
together. The stack keeps the reviewable units small and independent — one concern per PR, as ever
— while costing one arrival of attention rather than four.

*Write* is not *merge*. A PR whose merge must wait on something being observed still gets written,
reviewed and approved in this pass; what waits is its merge, and the thing that performs that
merge is a link in the chain (below), not a person's memory. Say so in that PR's body: what gates
it, and which queued step will merge it.

Approval of the stack is approval of the stack: it does not extend to a fix authored afterwards
(basics' *Acting on an approval to merge, ship or proceed*).

**3. Execution steps — a chain, not a checklist.** Once phase zero has landed the setup and the
approved stack has begun merging, the remaining steps run the migration: force the converge,
backfill the members, watch the cutover, merge the gated PR, retire the shim. If the first two
sorts were done properly there is no *approval* gate among them — but there is almost always a
**wait**, because each step's precondition is the previous step's effect becoming observable
somewhere the repo cannot see yet.

A wait is not a reason to write "then, later, do X". Every one of these steps is filed, at plan
time, as a queued continuation armed on the step before it. See **The chain** below.

That is the test of the plan. **Read the phases in order and mark every point where the run would
have to stop and wait for a person.** Each mark that falls after phase zero and the review pass is
a step that was sorted wrong — or a step that should have been a link in the chain and was written
as a note instead. Move it, chain it, or say in the plan why it genuinely cannot be either.

## The chain

Everything after the approval is a run that arms the next run. The mechanism is the queue's own
ad-hoc lane — the one `/do-later` and `verify-in-production` file into — and nothing here adds
machinery beside it: an ordinary issue, marked for the queue, carrying its own brief.

**File the whole chain when the plan is agreed**, not as each step falls due. One issue per
execution step, each naming the previous in `Blocked-by:`, so the queue does the waiting: a
blocked item is released when its blocker closes, which is exactly "the step before it finished".
Filing the chain up front is what makes it a mechanism rather than a habit — a chain that depends
on each run remembering to file its successor breaks silently the first time a run parks.

The chain's **last link is the plan's retrospective**, filed in the same pass with its brief
written now, while the design's expectations are still in front of you, `Blocked-by:` the final
execution step — so once the migration has lived in production for a while, something comes back
to read whether the design survived contact.
[production-retrospective](../production-retrospective/SKILL.md) owns what that brief answers and
its horizon.

Each link is a **sub-issue of the tracking issue** ([RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue
that belongs under another*), so the plan and its chain are one hierarchy read two ways rather
than two lists that can disagree. Where a link is a PR's merge rather than a run, that PR's body
closes **the link**, never the tracker: a phase PR carrying `Closes #<tracker>` ends the whole
migration on its first merge.

Each link's body is its whole brief, because the run that picks it up will never see the
conversation that planned it. Four things, and the first two are what make the link *chainable*:

- **What makes this step's world ready** — a thing to *read*, never a duration: a stamp, a file at
  a URL, an API answer. (`verify-in-production` spells this as `In-production-when:`, and a link
  that waits on a release rather than on the previous issue closing rides `Not-before:` +
  `Retry-every:` instead of `Blocked-by:`.)
- **What counts as this step having worked** — the assertion its own successor is waiting on.
  This is the load-bearing half: the chain advances on *validation*, not on the step having run.
- **The playbook**, exact enough to execute without judgment: what to do, and what to do when the
  check fails (comment what was read, leave the issue open — a failed step must not close, because
  closing is what releases the next link).
- **How it ends**: comment the evidence on the tracking issue, then close as completed. That close
  is the trigger for the next link, so it happens last and only on success.

Three hazards worth stating once:

- **Closing is the trigger, and nothing distinguishes a `completed` close from a `not planned`
  one.** Abandoning the migration means closing the *rest* of the chain first, tail-first; closing
  a link to tidy it away releases its successor into a world that is not ready.
- **A link that cannot make its reads must park, not guess.** A rate-limited or scope-blocked
  sweep answers "all clear" in exactly the way a healthy fleet does.
- **A chain is only as visible as its tracking issue.** Every link comments its result there, so
  the plan's checkboxes and the chain's state never have to be reconciled by hand.

## Writing it down

- **The plan is a tracking issue**, and the phases are its checkboxes. Status and remaining work
  live there; a design document, where the project keeps one, carries the mechanism and not the
  progress.
- **Each phase names its exit condition**, observable and stated as a thing that reads back true —
  not "cutover done" but "every member's stamp shows the new ref". A phase whose end is a judgment
  call is a phase that stays open.
- **Nothing closes on a human's memory.** A step you cannot verify now gets a mechanism that comes
  to you — a link in the chain, a scheduled task, an issue something converges (basics' *When
  verifying now is genuinely impossible*). A phase whose closing condition is "check next week" is
  not a phase.
- **Every execution phase names its link.** The checkbox says which issue runs it, so the plan and
  the queue are one thing read two ways rather than two lists that can disagree.
- **Size each step to what it is**, and don't restate in the plan what the design document or the
  linked issue already carries.

## Working through the plan

Once the plan is agreed, the issue body's plan is **append-only**. While implementing, scheduler run its
checkboxes and add below it — a comment, or a new section for what the work turned up — and never
edit, reword, condense or re-order what was already there.

The body is the record of what was agreed, and it is the only copy: an edit overwrites it in place
with nothing left to diff against, so a plan silently rewritten to match what was built reads
afterwards as a plan that was followed. Keeping it fixed is what makes the divergence visible —
and a divergence is the interesting part, not an embarrassment to tidy away.

So when the work shows a phase was wrong, say so **underneath**: what the plan assumed, what turned
out to be true, and what you did instead. If that changes the plan going forward, the new steps are
an addition, appended and dated; the superseded ones stay where they are, marked superseded rather
than deleted.

The exception is a **correction to the plan itself before implementation of it starts** — the owner
saying the plan misreads what they asked for. That is a correction (basics' *Acting on a
correction*): repair the body, since there is no work yet for it to have diverged from.

## Reviewing someone else's plan

Run the same sort over it. The findings worth raising, in order of what they cost:

1. A secret, permission, environment or account created **after** code that depends on it.
2. More than one review gate — two or more phases that each end in "open a PR and wait".
3. Code left unwritten because its phase is "later" — the cleanup and the destructive tail
   above all. Everything the migration will need is written and approved in the one pass; only
   merges and effects are deferred.
4. An execution step written as a note rather than filed as a link — anything phrased "then,
   once X, do Y" with no issue that comes back when X.
5. A chain whose links advance on a step having *run* rather than on its result being *read*.
6. A destructive step scheduled before the replacement has been observed working.
7. A phase with no stated exit condition, or one only a person can judge.
8. A step handed to a human that the agent could have performed itself.

input.title: Declarative task preconditions + the repo-active silence gate
input.body:
Give the `precondition` field a declarative expression form built on the automerge policy grammar (terms, `&&`, veto prefix, parameterized terms), with a built-in term vocabulary covering the shapes the 25 canon preconditions repeat — and a standard silence gate: no task runs on a silent repo unless its declaration says so explicitly, where a scheduled task's own PRs and commits count as silence.

Design (end state + rationale): `docs/task-preconditions/DESIGN.md` (Phase 1's PR).

Decisions taken at planning:
- Declarative form is additive; the `precondition` function stays legal forever and is the escape hatch for what no term expresses (`implement-request` stays code).
- Silence gate is an **explicit term per task** — every declarative precondition carries `unless:repo-silent` or the exemption marker `even-when-silent`, and the declaration-shape check enforces exactly one. No implied default.
- The four world-clock tasks (`rule-revalidation`, `prose-to-checks-sweep`, `jwt-advisory-watch`, `wiki-growth`) **get the gate** — they stop spending model runs on a repo nobody works in.
- Task-authored output is classified **structurally**: delivery lanes stamp a `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` commit trailer and the silence classifier keys on it (title regexes stay only for pre-trailer history).
- Fail direction inverts automerge: an unresolvable term or unreadable signal is `{ error }` — a loud run failure, never a quiet decline (F27, #1344's staleness asymmetry).

## Plan

No phase-zero out-of-band setup: every step is in-repo code, and no new secret, permission or platform setting is needed.

- [ ] **Phase 1 — design doc.** `docs/task-preconditions/DESIGN.md`: the expression grammar, the term vocabulary, the silence gate, alternatives with drawbacks. Exit: the doc is merged.
- [ ] **Phase 2 — evaluator.** `precondition-policy.mjs` beside `merge-policy.mjs`: parse + evaluate expressions over collected signals, auto-derive `precondition_signals`, auto-compose reason/context; `task-contract.mjs` accepts the expression form; `task-declaration-shape` validates it statically, including the presence of exactly one of `unless:repo-silent` / `even-when-silent`; tests (see-it-fail per term). Exit: suite green, a fixture declaration in each grammar shape validates and evaluates.
- [ ] **Phase 3 — the trailer + silence classifier.** `land-pr.mjs` / `deliver-generated.mjs` (and the queue's delivery path) stamp `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` on task-authored commits; the signal layer's substantive/repo-silent classification excludes trailer-carrying commits and PRs whose head commits carry it. Exit: a fixture task commit is classified silent, a plain human commit is not.
- [ ] **Phase 4 — convert the canon declarations.** All 24 convertible tasks (everything but `implement-request`) move to expressions, including gating the four world-clock tasks; pack version bumps + catalog rows + VERSIONS.md. Exit: `task-declaration-shape` green over the tree, sim/scenario tests green, no behavioural diff for the movement-gated tasks (the sim asserts it).
- [ ] **Phase 5 — verify live.** Force a scheduler run (`wake`) on a quiet state and on an active state; watch a gated task decline with the composed reason and an exempted one run. Exit: both verdicts observed in the run log, quoted here.
- [ ] **Phase 6 — retrospective.** After ~a week in production: did the silence gate decline the runs it was meant to (the world-clock tasks on quiet repos), did any task starve that shouldn't have, how many preconditions remain code. Filed per the production-retrospective skill when Phase 5 closes.

Phases 2–4 are written as one stacked pass and reviewed together (one approval, not three); Phase 5–6 chain behind the stack landing.

input.content:
# Declarative task preconditions

A task's `precondition` field accepts, beside the function form, a **declarative
expression**: data the engine evaluates over the collected signals, in the same
surface grammar the `automerge` policy field already taught every declaration —
named terms, a list as a union, `&&` as the intersection, a veto prefix, and
parameterized terms carrying an inline argument. The evaluator is a sibling of
the merge-policy engine (`packs/claudinite-tasks/precondition-policy.mjs` beside
`merge-policy.mjs`), and it runs at the one place a verdict has ever been formed:
the executor's pick (and the scheduler's planning read of the same function).

The function form stays legal forever. It is the escape hatch for a gate no term
expresses — `implement-request`'s push-permission eligibility is a security
boundary and stays code — and it is what a member's own local task files may
carry indefinitely, since nothing converges those.

Why data instead of code, when the function already works:

- **The repeated shapes stop drifting.** The canon's preconditions spell the same
  few gates — "substantive commit in the window", "declined while a PR of mine is
  pending", "movement or nothing" — in per-task code, each copy with its own
  null-handling and its own reason prose. A term is written once, with its
  three-valued semantics decided once.
- **A declaration becomes statically checkable.** The declaration-shape check can
  read an expression the way it reads an `automerge` policy: unknown terms,
  malformed arguments, and the silence-gate requirement below are all author-time
  findings. A function body is opaque to every check.
- **`precondition_signals` is derived, not declared.** Each term names the signals
  it reads, so a declarative task drops the field and the collector union can
  never disagree with what the gate actually consults. A function task keeps
  declaring it.

## The grammar

```
precondition: ['substantive-change', 'widen:issues-touched', 'unless:repo-silent']
```

- A **list is a union of reasons to run**: the run happens when any allow term is
  satisfied (and no veto matches), and the satisfied terms compose the verdict's
  `reason`. `&&` intersects parts within one term, exactly as in a merge policy.
- **`unless:<term>`** is a veto: a matching veto declines the run whatever the
  allow terms say. It is the mirror of the merge policy's `reject:`.
- **`widen:<term>`** contributes its scope and context only when another allow
  term already triggered — the grammar form of the corpus rule that a signal true
  most days may only widen an already-triggered run, so the rule is structural
  instead of remembered.
- **Parameterized terms** carry their argument inline after a colon, like
  `under:<dir>`: `unless:pr-touching:product-wiki/`,
  `paths-touched-outside:.claudinite/`.
- Terms marked **state** in the vocabulary (a presence, a configuration — facts
  true forever once true) are legal only inside an `&&` term or as a veto, never
  as a standalone allow term: the "gate on movement, never standing state" rule,
  enforced by the parser rather than by review.
- Each term contributes its share of `reason` and `context` (a touched-issue
  list, a member list, a capped path scope with an explicit dropped count), so
  the binding-scope lines today's preconditions hand-compose fall out of the
  terms.

## Fail direction: loud, never a quiet skip

This is the one deliberate inversion from the merge-policy engine. An automerge
policy that cannot be resolved fails closed to "nothing merges", which parks a PR
in front of a person — safe. A precondition that failed closed to "skip" would be
permanent, silent staleness: nothing in the repo goes red when a task stops
running. So an unknown term name, a malformed argument, or a term whose signal
is unreadable (`{ error }` on the signal, or a read the term needs that did not
resolve) returns `{ error }` — a failed run parked in the failure lane where the
re-queue lever retries it — never `{ run: false }`. A decline is a decision about
the world, and one taken on data that was not there is a guess whose cost is
unbounded.

## The term vocabulary

Built-in only. There is no pack-declared term file in this design (see
Alternatives): the residue that no built-in expresses keeps the function form.

Movement terms (may stand alone as allow terms):

| term | satisfied when | signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `always` | unconditionally — the manual levers ("an item exists, which is the request") and the fleet sweeps whose inputs no local signal can see | — |
| `substantive-change` | a substantive default-branch commit landed in the window | `commits` |
| `commits` | any default-branch commit in the window | `commits` |
| `session-captured` | a conversation log was stamped inside the window | `conversationLogs` |
| `issues-touched` | a non-task issue moved in the window (context: the touched set) | `issues` |
| `prs-touched` | an open PR was opened or updated in the window | `prs` |
| `mount-moved` | a declared pack's vendored files changed in the window (context: the packs) | `sharedMount` |
| `local-packs-changed` | the repo's local packs changed in the window | `localPacks` |
| `log-past-retention` | the oldest conversation log is older than the configured retention | `conversationLogs` |
| `manifest-ahead` | the shipped manifest version differs from the latest release tag | `release` |
| `fleet-local-packs-changed` | a participating member's local packs moved in the window (context: the member list, as binding scope) | `fleet` |
| `fleet-members` | the fleet has covered members (context: the member list) | `fleet` |
| `paths-touched-outside:<prefix>` | the window's commits touched paths outside `<prefix>` (context: the capped path list plus an explicit dropped count) | `commits` |

State terms (legal only in `&&` or as vetoes):

| term | asserts | signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local-packs-present` | the repo tracks local packs | `localPacks` |
| `stamp-present` | the mount exists (installed versions stamped) | `stamp` |
| `ships-pipeline` | the repo carries the release pipeline | `release` |
| `open-prs` | at least one PR is open | `prs` |

Vetoes:

| term | declines while | signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unless:repo-silent` | the repo is silent (below) | `commits`, `issues`, `prs`, `conversationLogs` |
| `unless:pr-titled:<prefix>` | an open PR's title starts with `<prefix>` — a previous round still pending | `prs` |
| `unless:pr-touching:<dir>` | an open PR changes a path under `<dir>`, **or an open PR's paths could not be read**: unknown is pending, because the veto exists so an unreviewed round is never stacked on one in flight | `prs` |

The fleet terms keep the current semantics of their code ancestors: a null
`fleet` signal (no PAT, not a canon home) and a fleet enumeration error both
decline with the reason naming which, since acting on unproven fleet state is
worse than a skipped sweep and the write-back problem of F27 does not apply to a
repo-local decline.

Worked conversions, spanning the grammar:

```
growth-extract:    ['substantive-change', 'unless:repo-silent']
tidy-issues:       ['issues-touched', 'widen:substantive-change', 'unless:repo-silent']
tidy-prs:          ['prs-touched && open-prs', 'unless:repo-silent']
growth-dedup:      ['mount-moved && local-packs-present', 'local-packs-changed', 'unless:repo-silent']
wiki-growth:       ['always', 'unless:pr-touching:product-wiki/', 'unless:repo-silent']
logs-prune:        ['log-past-retention', 'even-when-silent']
fleet-roster:      ['always', 'even-when-silent']
```

## The silence gate

**No task runs on a silent repo unless its declaration says so, explicitly.** A
repo is *silent* over a window when it saw no substantive commit, no non-task
issue touch, no non-task PR touch, and no captured session — where *a scheduled
task's own output counts as silence*: a task-authored PR merging, or its commits
landing, is the machinery running, not the project moving, and a fleet of tasks
must not keep each other awake.

Every **declarative** precondition must carry exactly one of:

- `unless:repo-silent` — the gate; or
- `even-when-silent` — a no-op marker term recording that this task deliberately
  runs on a silent repo.

The declaration-shape check enforces the pair's presence-or-exemption. There is
no implied default: a gate present by absence is a gate nobody decided, and the
marker is what makes the exemption visible in the one place a reader looks. A
**function** precondition is outside the check's reach — the function form is
itself the audited exception, and its author owns the gate.

The exemptions, and why each input is not the repo:

- the **manual levers** (`adopt-requested-packs`, `fleet-baseline`,
  `deploy-oauth-exchange`, `verify-production`) — a filed work item is the
  mandate; declining it closes an operator's own request unrun;
- **`update`** — its input is the canon, which moves when the repo does not, and
  a wrong decline is permanent staleness nothing in the member can repair;
- the **fleet sweeps** (`fleet-roster`, `fleet-pack-seeds`,
  `fleet-add-missing-packs`) — every input is another repo's tree;
- **`logs-prune`** — a clock crossing a retention boundary on an orphan branch;
- **`task-janitor`** — queue hygiene is about the queue, not the project.

The world-clock tasks — `rule-revalidation`, `prose-to-checks-sweep`,
`jwt-advisory-watch`, `wiki-growth` — carry the gate. Their *subject* is the
world (advisories publish, platforms move, research accrues), but their *value*
is zero on a repo nobody works in: a corrected rule nobody reads, an advisory
issue nobody sees, a wiki nobody opens. The first window with real activity
resumes them, which is also when their findings regain an audience.

### Classifying task output structurally

The silence classifier must not depend on what a task happened to title its PR.
Every delivery lane that commits on a task's behalf (`land-pr.mjs`,
`deliver-generated.mjs`, the queue's PR delivery) stamps a commit trailer:

```
Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>
```

The classifier reads silence off it: a commit carrying the trailer is silent,
and a touched or merged PR whose head commits carry it is silent — one commit

# Declarative task preconditions

A task's `precondition` field accepts, beside the function form, a **declarative
expression**: data the engine evaluates over the collected signals, in the same
surface grammar the `automerge` policy field already taught every declaration —
named terms, a list as a union, `&&` as the intersection, a veto prefix, and
parameterized terms carrying an inline argument. The evaluator is a sibling of
the merge-policy engine (`packs/claudinite-tasks/precondition-policy.mjs` beside
`merge-policy.mjs`), and it runs at the one place a verdict has ever been formed:
the executor's pick (and the scheduler's planning read of the same function).

The function form stays legal forever. It is the escape hatch for a gate no term
expresses — `implement-request`'s push-permission eligibility is a security
boundary and stays code — and it is what a member's own local task files may
carry indefinitely, since nothing converges those.

Why data instead of code, when the function already works:

- **The repeated shapes stop drifting.** The canon's preconditions spell the same
  few gates — "substantive commit in the window", "declined while a PR of mine is
  pending", "movement or nothing" — in per-task code, each copy with its own
  null-handling and its own reason prose. A term is written once, with its
  three-valued semantics decided once.
- **A declaration becomes statically checkable.** The declaration-shape check can
  read an expression the way it reads an `automerge` policy: unknown terms,
  malformed arguments, and the silence-gate requirement below are all author-time
  findings. A function body is opaque to every check.
- **`precondition_signals` is derived, not declared.** Each term names the signals
  it reads, so a declarative task drops the field and the collector union can
  never disagree with what the gate actually consults. A function task keeps
  declaring it.

## The grammar

```
precondition: ['substantive-change', 'widen:issues-touched', 'unless:repo-silent']
```

- A **list is a union of reasons to run**: the run happens when any allow term is
  satisfied (and no veto matches), and the satisfied terms compose the verdict's
  `reason`. `&&` intersects parts within one term, exactly as in a merge policy.
- **`unless:<term>`** is a veto: a matching veto declines the run whatever the
  allow terms say. It is the mirror of the merge policy's `reject:`.
- **`widen:<term>`** contributes its scope and context only when another allow
  term already triggered — the grammar form of the corpus rule that a signal true
  most days may only widen an already-triggered run, so the rule is structural
  instead of remembered.
- **Parameterized terms** carry their argument inline after a colon, like
  `under:<dir>`: `unless:pr-touching:product-wiki/`,
  `paths-touched-outside:.claudinite/`.
- Terms marked **state** in the vocabulary (a presence, a configuration — facts
  true forever once true) are legal only inside an `&&` term or as a veto, never
  as a standalone allow term: the "gate on movement, never standing state" rule,
  enforced by the parser rather than by review.
- Each term contributes its share of `reason` and `context` (a touched-issue
  list, a member list, a capped path scope with an explicit dropped count), so
  the binding-scope lines today's preconditions hand-compose fall out of the
  terms.

## Fail direction: loud, never a quiet skip

This is the one deliberate inversion from the merge-policy engine. An automerge
policy that cannot be resolved fails closed to "nothing merges", which parks a PR
in front of a person — safe. A precondition that failed closed to "skip" would be
permanent, silent staleness: nothing in the repo goes red when a task stops
running. So an unknown term name, a malformed argument, or a term whose signal
is unreadable (`{ error }` on the signal, or a read the term needs that did not
resolve) returns `{ error }` — a failed run parked in the failure lane where the
re-queue lever retries it — never `{ run: false }`. A decline is a decision about
the world, and one taken on data that was not there is a guess whose cost is
unbounded.

## The term vocabulary

Built-in only. There is no pack-declared term file in this design (see
Alternatives): the residue that no built-in expresses keeps the function form.

Movement terms (may stand alone as allow terms):

| term | satisfied when | signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `always` | unconditionally — the manual levers ("an item exists, which is the request") and the fleet sweeps whose inputs no local signal can see | — |
| `substantive-change` | a substantive default-branch commit landed in the window | `commits` |
| `commits` | any default-branch commit in the window | `commits` |
| `session-captured` | a conversation log was stamped inside the window | `conversationLogs` |
| `issues-touched` | a non-task issue moved in the window (context: the touched set) | `issues` |
| `prs-touched` | an open PR was opened or updated in the window | `prs` |
| `mount-moved` | a declared pack's vendored files changed in the window (context: the packs) | `sharedMount` |
| `local-packs-changed` | the repo's local packs changed in the window | `localPacks` |
| `log-past-retention` | the oldest conversation log is older than the configured retention | `conversationLogs` |
| `manifest-ahead` | the shipped manifest version differs from the latest release tag | `release` |
| `fleet-local-packs-changed` | a participating member's local packs moved in the window (context: the member list, as binding scope) | `fleet` |
| `fleet-members` | the fleet has covered members (context: the member list) | `fleet` |
| `paths-touched-outside:<prefix>` | the window's commits touched paths outside `<prefix>` (context: the capped path list plus an explicit dropped count) | `commits` |

State terms (legal only in `&&` or as vetoes):

| term | asserts | signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local-packs-present` | the repo tracks local packs | `localPacks` |
| `stamp-present` | the mount exists (installed versions stamped) | `stamp` |
| `ships-pipeline` | the repo carries the release pipeline | `release` |
| `open-prs` | at least one PR is open | `prs` |

| term | declines while | signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unless:repo-silent` | the repo is silent (below) | `commits`, `issues`, `prs`, `conversationLogs` |

`fleet` signal (no PAT, not a canon home) and a fleet enumeration error both
decline with the reason naming which, since acting on unproven fleet state is
worse than a skipped sweep and the write-back problem of F27 does not apply to a
repo-local decline.

wiki-growth:       ['always', 'unless:pr-touching:product-wiki/', 'unless:repo-silent']

input.body:
Phase 1 of #1572: `docs/task-preconditions/DESIGN.md` — the end state for a declarative `precondition` field.

- The expression grammar reuses the automerge policy surface: a list is a union of reasons to run, `&&` intersects, `unless:` vetoes, `widen:` marks a term that may only widen an already-triggered run, and state terms are conjunct-only by the parser.
- One built-in term vocabulary (~17 terms) covering the shapes the 24 convertible canon preconditions repeat; the `precondition` function stays legal forever as the escape hatch (`implement-request` stays code), and `precondition_signals` is derived from the expression.
- The fail direction inverts automerge: an unresolvable term or unreadable signal is `{ error }` — a loud run failure, never a quiet decline.
- The silence gate: every declarative precondition carries exactly one of `unless:repo-silent` / `even-when-silent`, check-enforced; a scheduled task's own output counts as silence via a `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` commit trailer the delivery lanes stamp.
- Alternatives with drawbacks: implied gate, hard engine gate, pack-declared terms, regex-only classification, status quo.

Closes #1573

The design doc is on the branch and [PR #1574](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1574) is open, closing slice issue [#1573](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1573); the plan lives in tracker [#1572](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1572).

**Summary of what this session established**

- **Yes, the automerge system generalizes cleanly.** The 25 canon preconditions decompose into ~17 repeating shapes: 11 are unconditional `run: true`, 9 are movement gates over the same few signal reads, plus pending-PR vetoes, thresholds, and fleet filters. Only `implement-request` (a security boundary) genuinely needs code — 24 of 25 convert to expressions like `['substantive-change', 'unless:repo-silent']`.
- **Two deliberate inversions from automerge**, both forced by existing lessons: an unresolvable expression is a loud `{ error }`, never a quiet skip (silent never-running is the expensive failure, per F27 and the update task's #1344 history); and the grammar gets `widen:` to structurally encode "a mostly-true signal may only widen an already-triggered run".
- **Your decisions, as recorded**: design-and-issue now with implementation later; the silence gate is an explicit per-task term (`unless:repo-silent` or `even-when-silent`, check-enforced, no implied default); the four world-clock tasks (rule-revalidation, prose-to-checks-sweep, jwt-advisory-watch, wiki-growth) get gated — the one real behavior change; and task output is classified silent via a structural `Claudinite-Task:` commit trailer, since today's title regexes would leak a plain-titled ci-performance or wiki-growth PR into "the repo moved".

```
docs/task-preconditions/ — new DESIGN.md: expression grammar, term vocabulary, silence gate, alternatives
```

> ⚠️ Still open: [PR #1574](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1574) awaits your review; implementation (phases 2–6 of [#1572](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1572)) is deferred to a later session — opener: `continue work on #1572`.
